[[RunningHead]]

Re-Visioning “Lacanian” Social Criticism: The Law and its Obscene Double

Slavoj Žižek

Slavoj Žižek

Slavoj Žižek   Researcher at the Institute of Social Sciences, University of Ljubljana and Visiting Fellow in the Department of English, Princeton University. His books include The Sublime Object of Ideology, For They Know Not What They Do, Looking Awry, Enjoy Your Symptom!, Tarrying with the Negative, The Metastases of Enjoyment, and, most recently, The Invisible Remainder: An Essay on Schelling and Related Matters.

My thesis is that what passes in American cultural criticism for “Lacanian theory” presents a very limited and distorted reception of Lacan's work. I want to challenge this established picture and render palpable another dimension of Lacan, far more productive for critical social theory.

The predominant feature of this established picture is the notion of Lacan as the phallogocentrist “philosopher of language” who emphasizes the price the subject has to pay in order to gain access to the symbolic order—all the false poetry of “castration,” of some primordial act of sacrifice and renunciation, of jouissance as impossible. So let's begin with this unfortunate castration.

In what, precisely, does symbolic castration consist? The trouble with the critics of Lacan's “phallocentrism” is that, as a rule, they refer to “phallus” or “castration” in a rather commonsense metaphoric way. In the standard feminist film studies, for example, every time a man behaves aggressively toward a woman or asserts his authority over her, one can be sure that his act will be designated as “phallic.” Likewise, every time a woman is framed, rendered helpless or cornered, one can be sure her experience will be designated as “castrating.”

What gets lost here is the paradox of the phallus itself as the signifier of castration: if we are to assert our (symbolic) “phallic” authority, the price to be paid is that we have to renounce the position of agent and consent to function as the medium through which the big Other—the symbolic institution—acts and speaks. When the subject is endowed with symbolic authority, he acts as an appendix of his symbolic title: it is the big Other who acts through him. Suffice it to recall a judge who is a miserable and corrupted person, but the moment he puts on his robe and other insignia, his words are the words of Law itself.

It's the same with paternal authority: a real father exerts authority only insofar as he posits himself as the embodiment of a transcendent symbolic agency, insofar as he accepts that it is not himself, but the big Other who speaks through him, in his words. Recall the millionaire from a film by Claude Chabrol who inverts the standard complaint about being loved only for his millions: “If only I could find a woman who would love me for my money and not for myself!

Psychoanalysis and Social Identity, or the Pyrrhic Victory of Hysteria

Judith Gurewich

Judith Gurewich

Judith Gurewich   Practices psychoanalysis in Cambridge, MA, and teaches a seminar on Lacan at the Center for Literary and Cultural Studies at Harvard University. She is affiliated with the Boston Psychoanalytic Institute and is an active member of Espace Analytique, a psychoanalytic institute in Paris. She has published articles in French and English on various topics related to psychoanalysis and the social sciences. She is presently editing a collection entitled The Subject and the Self and is Editor of a new series, “The Lacanian Clinical Field,” at Jason Aronson.

I would like to argue that the “post-colonial” ethos that is pervasive today in Lacanian-influenced feminist and cultural studies is equally at work in contemporary American psychoanalysis. While some sophisticated trends in feminist theory have emphasized the power of hysterical resistance as a factor for social change, new perspectives in American psychoanalysis have been promoting a model of a self no longer compelled to adopt the ideals of the phallocratic system. In both cases, the most radical insights of the Freudian discovery have been eclipsed, and as a result the repressed has returned in an unexpected way. While the modern psychoanalyst—who has declared hysteria obsolete—unknowingly favors in Monsieur Jourdain fashion the demand of the hysteric over her or his desire, the “Lacanian” theorist seems to promote the hysterical structure as the desirable new paradigm of subjectivity. This shift, while emotionally, socially, and culturally productive, nevertheless ignores the function of symbolic castration as a condition of communication and creativity.

As a social theorist turned psychoanalyst, I would like first of all to offer my condolences to my ex-colleagues—i.e., the neo-Marxists and neo-Weberians of today—who are now pressed to swallow heavy doses of Lacan if they want to catch up with the present expertise of those who have taken on what is currently called cultural studies and the post-colonial ethos: that is, a no-man's-land for sure, a woman's land maybe, but certainly a land where the subject is no longer the master of its own house, where the ego has fallen off the horse of the id, and where our beloved category of the social has been scribbled over with the graffiti of signifiers without meanings.

I don't want to be conservative; I have no intention of gluing the subject back together with the belief that as human beings we can be responsible for what we are and what we do. Yet the function of psychoanalysis as a factor for social change must be approached with a lot of circumspection. For when we come right down to it, a few painful Borromean knots later, what did Lacan bring to the field of social theory that was not already said—and better said—by Marx, Weber, Durkheim and the Frankfurt School? Can the Symbolic, the Imaginary, and the Real be adequately extended beyond the frontiers of the analytic situation? Can they accurately describe the forces at work in the social realm? Can they go beyond resolving the old dichotomy between nature and culture that has plagued theories of subjectivity for centuries? Can psychoanalysis truly promote social change, or can it only explain retroactively how each individual has come to be “carried” by an ideology that camouflages (in the best of cases) the division he or she had to endure in order to survive as a social being? Once we have said that, then what? Can psychoanalysis be anything other than one more critical grid that helps us distinguish, as Žižek puts it, the hidden mechanisms that regulate social visibility and non-visibility?

Law

Law's Appropriations of Psychoanalysis

David Caudill

David Caudill

David Caudill   Associate Professor of Law at Washington and Lee University, is co-editor of Radical Philosophy of Law and author of Lacan and the Subject of Law: Toward a Psychoanalytic Critical Legal Theory.

The discipline of law is consciously interdisciplinary these days—the named sub-disciplines of law and economics, women and the law, law and religion, law and literature (or language, or interpretation), law and medicine (or psychology), and law and society are well-established, and all have their own associations and journals. Of course, law has always been interdisciplinary, not only in the obvious sense that jurisprudence, legal history, and the sociology of law necessarily involve philosophers, historians, and sociologists, but also in the sense that legal processes and institutions reproduce, sometimes unwittingly, particular views of politics, religion, interpretation, women, the economy, and science. Now that the links between law and other disciplines are being acknowledged and discussed with greater frequency, some theoretical frameworks, like economics, are decisively influential (e.g., in policy debates and judicial opinions), many, like literary theory, are recognized as the source of minor insights (e.g., in debates over interpretation of legal texts), and a few, like radical feminist theory, are viewed with predictable suspicion.

The degree of influence and acceptance of psychoanalysis within contemporary legal theory, education, and practice parallels the influence and acceptance of psychoanalysis within social theory and clinical psychology or psychiatry generally. That is, since clinical psychoanalysis is in crisis (Chalfin & Rosenblitt), seen by many psychiatrists as a thing of the past, that state of affairs is mirrored in legal processes and institutions. When courts require up-to-the-minute scientific expertise on questions of mental capacity, an argument claiming that certain knowledge was repressed will be ridiculed, and “Law and Psychiatry” textbooks (e.g., Spring et al.) will no longer include a chapter on psychoanalysis. On a happier note, since the use of psychoanalytic theory is alive and well in critical social theory and cultural studies, that state of affairs is also present in the work of critical legal theorists. Thus, while the explanatory power of psychoanalysis for “clinical” questions of law—e.g., testamentary capacity, capacity to contract, the insanity defense, or custody and civil commitment standards—is now minimal, the tradition of social psychoanalysis continues to address questions of how law works through (1) its images of collectivity, rationality, and neutrality, (2) its interpretive paradigms, and (3) its repression and denial of its politics, its formalism, and its conventionalism. In short, while psychoanalysis has become irrelevant in law on the clinical-legal issues in regard to which it has obvious expertise to contribute, psychoanalysis continues to enter the discourse of law through the back door of social theory as a means of revealing and critiquing the foundations of law.

Management

“Identity” and Anxiety in the Contemporary Workplace

O. McSwite

O. McSwite

O. McSwite   Pseudonym for Orion F. White, Professor of Public Administration at Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, and Cynthia J. McSwain, Associate Professor of Public Administration at George Washington University. Together they have over forty years of experience working as consultants of all types in the United States and internationally. They have published widely on the subjects of organizational change and psychological and social theory.

Psychoanalysis has a great deal to say to the field of organizations and management, as it would to any field which emphasizes the preeminence of the conscious attitude to such an overweening degree. Management theory is beset with a number of rather large anomalies that have, for the most part, been ignored. For example, despite a large and rich literature in organizational sociology that solidly undermines the notion of rational control, management theorists remain wedded to the idea that such control is possible. The existence of anomalies like this one suggests that management theory is not grounded in science or even technique as much as it is in ideology. A psychoanalytic perspective suggests that what maintains this ideology is the unconscious gratifications that it produces more than its effectiveness in increasing productivity.

A prime example of this is the use of performance evaluations. There is a long line of empirical research indicating that worker performance evaluation not only does not improve performance but positively impairs it, by creating a net outcome of demotivation among the worker group. This finding is echoed loudly by practical managerial experience.

Identity Consolidation in Zines

Fred Wright

Fred Wright

Fred Wright   Doctoral student in English at Kent State University. He studied zines for his master's thesis, “Personality on Parade: A Psychoanalytic Analysis of the Zine Revolution.” He also plays guitar in a punk rock band called the Hot Glue Guns.

Over the past two decades, independent small-run publications known as zines have become increasingly common. Produced by a single individual or a small group, zines focus on subjects of personal importance to the publisher, whether it be punk rock, bowling, the collection of pez dispensers, or the zine publisher's daily life. Created by methods ranging from handwriting to computer desktop publishing programs, and published by photocopying or offset printing, zines are usually distributed in a folksy, haphazard manner that often includes the US Postal Service, dropoffs at local record or book stores, and gifts to friends and family. Frequently irreverent and usually appealing to audiences with highly specialized interests, zines were once considered strictly a fringe phenomenon. In the last few years, though, zines have emerged into the mainstream of American culture. Now they are sold at large bookstore chains such as Tower, Borders, and Barnes and Noble and are celebrated in articles and featured in mainstream media. Currently, the number of zines is estimated to be between 20,000 and 50,000, and with the advent of e-zines and home pages on the Internet and World Wide Web, even more people are expected to begin publishing their own zines in coming years.

The fantastic growth of zines has usually been attributed to the increased accessibility and widespread use of communication technology such as the personal computer, desktop publishing software, and the photocopier.

The End of the Welfare State and the Postmodern Subject

Juha Siltala

Juha Siltala

Juha Siltala   Senior Researcher at the Renvall Institute for Historical Studies at the University of Helsinki. He completed his doctoral degree in 1985 on the Finnish Fascist movement in 1930 and since then has studied Finnish psychohistory and culture. His study of pietism in the first half of 19th century as the first form of individual subjectivity of common men appeared in 1992, and in 1994 he published a monograph on male shame and social competence in modern society. He is presently studying the forbidden aspects of self during the national awakening and the Finnish Civil War.

Work has traditionally been the way for Finnish men to bring their feelings into balance and to meet other people without fear of being re-engulfed by their emotional requirements. The end of the full-employment society has obliged them to rebuild their self-systems afresh. This crisis in the regulation of self-feeling can cause one of two reactions: either it can increase a man's freedom to redefine his relation to his inner compulsions to repeat, or it can lead to a skinheadlike reaction of projective identification.

Jeffrey Berman's Diaries to an English Professor is a totally unique book. I know of no equivalent study in either literary, pedagogical, or psychoanalytic literature. Never before has there been an attempt to track as extensively over time the self-representations of students writing within a classroom situation informed by a psychoanalytic method. Berman, Professor of English at the State University of New York at Albany, has undertaken a true tour-de-force. The book records, with the students' acquiescence, the change in student self-representation in the self-reflective diaries that Berman encourages his English-literature students to keep as part of his ongoing class on literature and psychoanalysis. More than a decade of material is digested in this book, which shows a rich and deep understanding of the relationship between historical change and underlying constitutional and psychological structures.

Berman has four themes at the center of his work: the study of relationship to dissolving parental authority, eating and its disorders, suicide, and sexuality. These are central topics for the age group (between eighteen and twenty-two) that Berman is examining, and they are concepts that undergo a substantial shift in importance and emphasis during the 1980s and early 1990s. Berman's book enables the reader to examine how these topics are internalized as the public discourse about the nuclear family, anorexia, student suicide, and sexuality in the age of AIDS come to be front-page (or at least primetime) concerns of American culture.

Berman's approach is that of a teacher of literature rather than that of a sociologist or psychologist. He deals with texts, with the diaries that his students prepare as a classroom assignment. Yet he makes the point early on that the diary entries seem to be better written than the actual compositions the students write. I find this revealing. It does seem that when topics are addressed that are meaningful for students, their engagement increases. This is a major pedagogical tool that has as much relevance for graduate as for undergraduate education.

Joseph Smith MD

Joseph Smith

Joseph Smith   Founding editor of the Psychiatry and the Humanities Series (1976-93). Prior to retirement he was Supervising and Training Analyst at the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

My topic is original evil, not radical evil. I focus, that is, on early development with the aim of depicting as nearly as possible the very first staging of the negative. In psychoanalysis, the negative refers to aggression, the death instinct, primitive guilt, depression, the negative therapeutic reaction, characters wrecked by success, the repetition compulsion, and suicide, and how forms of self-negation, self-disavowal, and self-destruction can be transmuted into forms of outer-directed violence, exploitation, and proneness to radical evil. Each of these negative outcomes of development is the subject of a vast domain of study. Not one of them could be encompassed by even the most valid formulation of original evil. Nevertheless, if there be an original common matrix in which all forms of the negative begin, a clearer way of thinking about that origin might shed light on the different paths leading toward each of the negative positions listed. It is also my hope, although I barely touch on such applications, that a better understanding of vicissitudes of the negative in individual development will help to clarify similar phenomena encountered at a societal level.

The points I want to make and the questions I raise in this paper are as follows:

Original evil is original danger that will come to be known as inner danger.

Flight from inner danger takes the form of focusing on an image of the object, an object imagistically remembered and anticipated as providing resolution of danger, a not-yet object that will come to be known as other, as outer.

The cry is initially a crying against inner danger and only later a call for the mother. Primal aggression begins as attack on the not-yet self and not, as Laplanche has suggested, in “aggressiveness that is directed outward” (Life and Death 90). Primal aggression precedes autoerotism.

We can take Freud's concept of the death instinct as biological and pronounce him wrong, as did Lacan, in at least one important passage (Ecrits 8), or we can read Freud, as I do, in terms of what he called “the biological view” of instinct. In that view a bodily imbalance is a demand on the mind for work, but instinct per se is in and of the psyche, the first level of psychic response to the bodily demand as inner danger (Freud, “Instincts and Their Vicissitudes” 121-22; see also Loewald, “On Motivation” 116-117 and “Instinct Theory” 208).

Although most of the recent public attention on suicide has focused on physician-assisted death, youth suicide remains a grave national problem. The suicide rate for adolescents 15-19 years of age has quadrupled in the last 40 years; suicide is now the second leading cause of death among people in this age group. Even more disturbing are the results of the national school-based Youth Risk Survey, sponsored by the United States Centers for Disease Control (CDC). The survey indicated that 27 percent of all American high school students thought seriously about committing suicide in 1990; 8 percent of all students actually attempted suicide; and 2 percent of all students sustained injuries in the course of a suicide attempt serious enough to warrant medical attention. Each year over a quarter of a million high school students make at least one suicide attempt requiring hospitalization—a staggering figure.

How can educators reduce youth suicide? The CDC concluded its study by recommending a variety of strategies, including educating youths about the warning signs of suicide and about the availability of suicide prevention services. The recommendation is consistent with the 1989 Report of the Secretary's Task Force on Youth Suicide.

[E]fforts to reduce suicide by improving the general coping skills of high risk youth—e.g., helping youth to recognize and talk about their feelings, ask for help when needed, identify how and where to get help for oneself and others—should be beneficial in preventing a wide range of problem behaviors. (38)

And yet given the pervasiveness of suicidal thinking and the need for public education, self-inflicted death remains a tabooed subject inside and outside of the classroom. It is easy to understand why students may feel uncomfortable talking about suicide; but it is less easy to understand why literature teachers are reluctant to bring up the subject, especially when reading novels, poems, or plays containing suicidal characters. Teachers often avoid discussing the suicides of Edna Pontellier in Kate Chopin's The Awakening and of Septimus Warren Smith in Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, despite the fact that these deaths are the central actions of both novels. Many teachers seem reluctant to tell their students that Sylvia Plath and Anne Sexton took their own lives, even though both poets return repeatedly to this subject in their writings.

Sometimes it seems that the more the blurring of national and ethnic boundaries delivers us into a racial and cultural collage, the more sealed up we become in ethnically specific perceptions of reality, so that multicultural living resembles more a collision of soliloquies, to borrow Clifford Geertz's phrase (120), than it does a fruitful dialogue across ethnic and cultural lines. My object here is to explore some problematics of communication between academic women of different ethnic and cultural backgrounds, not by addressing the historical context of power relations in which our present-day relations are inevitably embedded and the racially skewed economic and political structures in which we live, but by rethinking the psychological processes of identification and idealization that apparently impede communication between women of different racial and cultural backgrounds. While these historical and material conditions no doubt pose more formidable obstacles to trust and understanding than the psychological processes I will be exploring, the exchanges that I cite between some white academic feminists and the scholars of color whom they idealize show that unconscious processes of identification and idealization can also lead to misunderstanding. In discussing the way that white feminists Elizabeth Abel, Jane Gallop, Tania Modleski, and Jane Stembridge appear to be idealizing African American women, I am continuing a process that they themselves have initiated. For in writing about their projections of a liberated power and authority onto African American women, these white women are both describing one of the obstacles to genuine dialogue—an idealizing vision of the other woman that does not take into account her complexity as a subject—and contributing to an analysis of the white middle-class female position. That contribution is especially valuable because it adds to the conscious intentions of white women the unconscious fantasies and quirks of perception produced by our own construction in race, class, and gender discourses. And moving idealizing fantasies of the other woman from the private world of static fantasy to the public space of the printed text enables us to work with them, perhaps clearing the way for more productive dialogues.

Psychoanalysis and Ideology Critique

It is by now perhaps a truism to state that psychoanalytic and postcolonial critiques are unlikely bedfellows. We have only to glance at the bulk of post-colonial scholarship to note the near absence of psychoanalysis as a theoretical tool that would enable a postcolonialist to unloosen the bindings of colonial and neocolonial history.1 The grand récit of the Freudian family romance, compelling enough on its own terms when confined in the life of the ego to its relations among the family socius, reads differently in another, thoroughly ideologically inflected register. According to the materialist, historically specific ideology critique that characterizes most current post-colonial scholarship in the fields of English and cultural studies, psychoanalysis seems suspiciously universalist, dehistoricized, and Western-imperialist in its production of a truth and a subject that can seem to evade the reach of ideology, history, empire, and nation. Admittedly, this line of thinking tends toward reductionism. Still, one must call attention to the striking absence, in psychoanalysis, of a full or even adequate study of the gendered subaltern and her role in the class struggle for autonomy and self-determination in the margins of the narratives of nation and self.2 It is the absence of such a materialist analysis that causes Ania Loomba to critique the universalizing tendencies in the feminist psychoanalytic theories espoused by, among others, Julia Kristeva. As she puts it,

so much of linguistic and semiotic theory brushes, often via psychoanalysis, perilously close to universalist assumptions about the nature of subversion and thereby about the repressed and rebellious subject. The specific inputs into protest need not be examined, hence woman becomes a category that need admit of little differentiation….

[T]he neglect of histories surrounding native insubordination either devalues or romanticizes the latter, or worse, tends to read colonized subjects through linguistic or psychoanalytical theories which remain suspiciously and problematically shot through with ethnocentric assumptions whose transfer to all subalterns is unacceptable. (307)

Research into the social and psychological “causes” of rape was once so meager that one had to assume that rape was either uncommon or so successfully hidden that it could escape the notice of psychologists and other concerned professionals. It was not until Susan Brownmiller's pioneering feminist work on rape, Against Our Will, that a large number of psychologists specifically addressed the significance of rape or its startling prevalence in the United States. Since Brownmiller's text in the 1970s, a plethora of psychological studies has appeared. Some simply gather epidemiological data (e.g., Koss 35-49). Others attempt to characterize the perpetrators of rape or to assess its effects on victims (Scully and Marolla 63-70; Pollard 60-64; Warshaw 65-82). There is also abundant literature on the development and implementation of rape prevention programs, most especially in secondary and post secondary education (Berkowitz 35-36). In concert with feminist initiatives in the development of rape crisis centers, in the theorization of rape, and in changes in the legal system, psychological research and applications presently make critical contributions to contemporary discourses and programs that address rape.

With respect to the study of rape, the relationship between psychoanalysis and psychology replicates the more general relationship between the two fields. Although psychology owes much to psychoanalysis, both clinically and conceptually, the discipline is quite suspicious of psychoanalytic approaches.

The question of addiction has become a central problematic at the end of the Twentieth Century. Alcoholism and substance abuse are now considered to be social as well as personal modes of behavior that transcend the boundaries between individual psychology and public policy In his article “The Rhetoric of Drugs,” Jacques Derrida argues that addictions can no longer be conceptualized as natural phenomena. Rather, to understand drugs, “a history is required, and a culture, conventions, evaluations, norms, an entire network of intertwined discourses” (2). As in the case of the analysis of gender, we must begin to look at the way that addictions are constructed culturally in moral and ethical discourses.

In order to stress the “diction” in addiction, many theorists have turned away from an essentialist definition of drugs and have begun to articulate a theory of the social construction of substance abuse. However, at the same time that there has been a move toward theorizing drugs as a cultural discourse, there has also been an opposite movement toward seeing drugs as a method of escaping from the social and symbolic order of language and convention. In this view, addictions are a cultural construct that attempts to refuse cultural mediation itself. The more that one attempts to symbolize the structure of drug addiction, the more the drug addict attempts to remove him or herself from the symbolic order.

In many ways the discourse of Twelve-Step Programs participates in this movement toward constructing a social knowledge of and on addiction by helping the addicted subject to forge a new social bond that calls for his or her submission to the Great Other. Whether it is God, or the sponsor, or the drug, or the community of fellow addicts, members of groups like Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) are called to subject themselves to the dominance of a discourse that surrounds them. The result of this structure is what Foucault might call a new form of community-based confession.

The subtitle of MacCannell's book, After the Patriarchy, may be understood in either of two ways: what has happened after the Enlightenment's overthrow of monarchical government and of the father's domination, or what is to happen, given that patriarchy has not released its hold. Juliet Flower MacCannell is pointing to the irony of modernity, in claiming to have removed hierarchical oppression and replaced it with democratic sovereignty, when the result has been the exposure of the continuing oppression of those for whom patriarchy has no definition, the literally and metaphorically colonized: the native, and the woman.

MacCannell's view is expressed in the form of a cogent dictum, that the role of the Father has been subtly reoccupied by the Brother. The primal father has been killed, but his power has been transferred to his sons. Patriarchy is as powerful as ever, and part of its power lies in the nature of its disguise, that of democratic equality and individual liberty, purveyed and maintained by the third of the Enlightenment triad, fraternity. Despite its positive connotations, the fraternal is a patriarchal term: “liberty, equality, and sorority” sounds distinctly odd to our sexist ears. It is the continuing gloss of these ideals that hides their inadequacies from oppressor and oppressed. MacCannell argues that modernity's emphasis on individual equality becomes an effacement of otherness, and that its emphasis on the sovereign subject becomes an empowerment of the male fraternal individual. After MacCannell, one could coin a new word, “fraternalism.” The Brother is now characterized by what Lacan called repression of the recognition of the other.

The material MacCannell enlists to uphold her thesis is both literary and psychoanalytic, the literature interlocked with history. She detects in Rousseau the hidden flaw of the ideal of a democratic collective “self,” expressed in a faultless “general will,” repressing recognition of the other (sex). Rousseau admired Geneva, which, like Sparta, excluded women from positions of power. MacCannell, however, can cite Rousseau the novelist against Rousseau the political theorist as one who is capable of ironizing bourgeois marriage, for in Julie, ou la Nouvelle Héloïse he can show how the daughter's desire is ignored in her very acceding to male ethical demands. Neither the daughter nor the mother is allowed to install a superego.

Psychoanalytic Theory: An Introduction is the second of four books by Anthony Elliott, Research Fellow in political science at the University of Melbourne, each one surveying the contemporary field of psychoanalytic social and cultural theory and critique. Elliott's earlier Social Theory & Psychoanalysis in Transition: Self and Society from Freud to Kristeva (Blackwell, 1992) seems to be the expanded version of Psychoanalytic Theory, the two books are organized almost identically, but Psychoanalytic Theory is by contrast a summation—fewer theorists are discussed and fewer details of the theories presented are included. Elliott's third book, co-edited with Stephen Frosh, is a collection of essays entitled Psychoanalysis in Contexts: Paths between Theory and Modern Culture (Routledge, 1995); contributors include Elliott, Frosh, some of the major theorists discussed in Elliott's first two books (Castoriadis, Chodorow, J. Benjamin, Kovel, Sprengnether, Rustin), and others (Sayers, Segal, Dews, Macey). The redundancy I identify is intended not as a criticism, but as an indication that Psychoanalytic Theory is indeed an introduction and that substantial elucidations of Elliott's views and of some of those he introduces are available in the other two books.

Elliott seeks a middle ground for psychoanalytic social theory between traditional and postmodern psychoanalytic strategies. Traditionally, the “focus on self-mastery and adaptation in ego psychology” (21) leads to an uncritical social conformism, while the tendency in object relations theory “to project self-development as the unfolding of a human essence” (24) ends up politically conservative. Passions of the Voice is a powerful synthesis and elaboration of Claire Kahane's prior contributions to the field of feminist psychoanalytic criticism. Developing the historico-theoretical interest in hysteria announced in Kahane's co-edited collection In Dora's Case (Bernheimer) as well as the maternal fantasms set forth in the equally influential volume, The (M)other Tongue (Garner), Kahane's new single-authored book maps the aesthetic, historical, and theoretical vectors linking the problem of voice to the formal and pathological outlines of hysteria in late Victorian and early modernist literature. Kahane's title phrase “passions of the voice” names the suffering and fragmentation undergone by the female subject as she enters into and falls out of the symbolizing possibilities of speech. The concept of “voice” here covers much terrain, offering a flexible category that accommodates Kahane's associative interpretive style: it includes narrative voice, the speech of the mother in infancy, the “talking cure” of psychoanalysis, the cry of the child, and the rise of the female orator in the suffrage movement, as well as the shifting oppositions between speech and writing, hearing and seeing, and music and poetry. The result is an evocative, often masterful recreation of a world of discourse marked by the trauma of maternal loss, the catastrophe that both motivates and stymies the search for a viable feminine subject position within the Oedipal order.

The book is least successful in its attempt to “historicize” this subjective crisis. The opening chapter linking the rise of modern feminism to that of hysteria as a clinical category relies almost exclusively on recent secondary sources for its account of medical and political developments in the period; as with so many recent historicist approaches, Kahane relies on a series of exhausted citations and stereotypes that threaten to reify the epistemological and political complexities of Victorian medical and political culture. For example, Kahane's rapid leap from the “breathless” devotion of Alice James' mother to the constricting corsets worn by nineteenth-century women (43) manifests the kind of sound-bite historicism that has too often stood in for archival work in recent years. So, too, the attempt to unify the chapters around the figure of the female orator never really creates the “materialist” coherence it is purported to do; of the literary narratives examined, only Henry James' The Bostonians directly engages the cultural fantasy of the suffragette. Kahane's decision to revisit the Dora case instead of that of “Anna O.” (the social activist Bertha Pappenheim) indicates that Kahane's real interests are finally literary more than historical, narratological more than materialist.

This past June, I had the good fortune to be involved in a weekend retreat and conference on spirituality and psychoanalysis at Mt. Ranier. This meeting, organized by the Northwest Center for Psychoanalysis, was a pioneering effort to encourage serious reflection on the relationship between discourses on subjects that normally proceed in two unrelated (and sometimes antagonistic) universes. Assuming that this state of affairs hurts psychoanalysis, the planning committee invited psychoanalysts from different religious backgrounds to present their ideas. I am very pleased to have been included in this event, which evidently was enormously satisfying for everyone who attended.

Dixie Noble, PhD, a Native American psychoanalyst from Los Angeles, asserted that a keen respect for symbolism is intrinsic to the spiritual tradition of the Native American peoples. She and her colleague Curtis Kekahbah described rituals such as mask-making and the sweat-lodge ceremony. According to Dr. Noble, the healing that comes from participation in such activities resembles the healing that psychoanalysis offers because both religious ritual and psychoanalytic process promote a sense of unity and integration. Religious ritual promotes a sense of unity with respect to the cosmos, while psychoanalysis promotes unity of and within the psyche.

Beverly Gorsuch, MRE, MSW, a graduate of Yale Divinity School and one of the founders of the Northwest Center for Psychoanalysis, described Moses, Buddha, Jesus, Catherine of Sienna, Yogananda, Ghandi, and Mother Teresa as “spiritual giants … [who] rattle our cages.” She said they “validate and radically expand our psychoanalytic views of human capacity…. They go heroically deeper into the very processes all humans use.” She originally went into psychoanalysis for help with pain, but, finding limited relief from psychoanalysis, she renewed and extended her religious commitment-without abandoning psychoanalysis.

Tibetan Buddhism, according to Lobsang Rapgay, PhD (who could not be present), aims for the same thing as psychoanalysis, a kind of reparation that he describes in terms of psychological individuation and “inner peace.

Patricia Elliot

Patricia Elliot   Teaches Sociology and Women's Studies at Wilfrid Laurier University in Waterloo, Ontario. She is author of From Mastery to Analysis: Theories of Gender in Psychoanalytic Feminism and is currently exploring the implications of transgender theories for contemporary conceptions of gender.

Over the last decade, theoretical and political crises within North American women's movements and within feminist theory have produced a recognition of the need for more productive dialogue about racist discourses and practices. Several impasses have made addressing this need difficult. Three of these impasses will be discussed here by way of introducing this paper, a paper which occupies a particular position historically and politically due to its relationship to these impasses. These three impasses concern how what Homi K. Bhabha calls “the Other question” should be addressed, whether analyses of racism as a set of economic, cultural, and political arrangements should take precedence over analyses of subjective investments in racism, and who ought to speak to these issues.

With respect to the first impasse, white women have been criticized for failing to address women of color as well as for engaging in other forms of racist discourse. But if, as bell hooks claims, “Black people are not born into this world with innate understanding of racism and white supremacy” (118), then it would be foolish to assume that white people automatically possess such an understanding. As a white, middle-class woman, I find Elizabeth Spelman's analysis of racist discourse an excellent source for understanding how and why racism is so easily reproduced, and not only by whites.1 Learning how to address the “other” requires work.

The second impasse concerns the focus of analysis and probably poses the greatest challenge, rooted as it is in a series of false oppositions between “objective” and “subjective,” social and psychic, institutional and personal. While a systematic analysis of racism (like other major social divisions) obviously requires an understanding of the social, political, and economic processes through which it is produced and maintained, it also requires an understanding of the subjective investments of various social groups in those processes.2 One of the reasons for neglecting the latter (particularly the investment of dominant groups in racist discourses), is that subjective investments become equated with “attitudes” that are supposedly easily changed and that are mistakenly believed to substitute for collective and institutional social change.3 A preoccupation with changing attitudes can be seen, for example, in some antiracist consciousness-raising sessions where, according to Arun Mukherjee, “one self-flagellates in public” (170).4 Clearly, one needs to avoid a romanticized, self-congratulatory or self-deprecatory stance that both begins and ends with acknowledgement of complicity in racist society. Such a confessional stance, however, should not be confused with the “education for critical consciousness” that bell hooks urges us to develop, which involves both understanding and transforming subjective investments in racist discourse (hooks 118). The development of a critical consciousness requires a different kind of analysis than that which deals exclusively with political, economic, and cultural relations. It requires an analysis of how processes of subjectification occur within those relations. I contend that an understanding of these processes in relation to their colonial or racist contexts is necessary for the achievement of antiracist goals.5 Such a contention on my part raises the question of authorship, which brings me to the third impasse.

Time is elusive and difficult to keep in perspective. In an effort to see it clearly, I sometimes remind myself that the 1960s are as distant from the 1990s as the 1930s were from the 1960s. This is especially helpful, or rather especially necessary, when communicating with my students, whose formative experiences are so disjoined from my own. Recently, however, I've begun to believe that the comparison understates the disjunction.

We might think of it this way. Capitalist economies are structured by the relationship between capital and wage-labor. This structural relationship has been paralleled or mediated by the opposition of working class (leftist) and capitalist (rightist) political tendencies. Moreover, at least since the time of the industrial revolution, the Left has been pulled forward by the hope of progressing beyond the stage of capitalist development. One might even say that these three elements (the economic relationship of wage-labor and capital, the Left-Right political axis, and the project of going beyond capitalism) are constitutive of modernity.

If this view is accepted, then the 1930s and the 1960s were modern times. Hence the appropriateness of the designations, Old Left and New Left. The 1990s are no longer modern in this sense. At least in the United States, there no longer is an effective left opposition to capitalist domination, nor the hope of bringing the capitalist era to an end. “No longer” does not mean “never again.” But for the moment, we are living in postmodern times.1

We can date the advent of this postmodern period quite precisely. The fall of the Berlin wall in 1989 symbolized the end of the Cold War as we knew it, and of the Soviet Union as the political counterweight to the United States and its allies. The world abruptly became unipolar. To be sure, and as convergence theorists had long argued, the ideological opposition of East and West may have been more apparent than real. Nonetheless the bipoiarity of world powers created a space for class struggle and the politics of inter-class compromise. And the existence of a place outside of capitalism animated the belief in a time after it, even if Soviet realities had almost nothing in common with socialist ideals. Then, when the Soviet sphere collapsed, capitalism was all that remained. Deprived of the hope of transcending capitalism, the Left withered away; and as its power and promise faded, left liberalism and then even centrist liberalism rapidly followed. At least for now, and at least in the United States, capitalism runs unopposed.

Can a psychoanalytic perspective shed light on Mexico's recent Indian revolt? Are psychoanalytic concepts useful tools for understanding the conflict in Chiapas, which has shaken the entire country to a degree far beyond the scope of the events themselves?

We must recognize the dangers attendant upon transferring psychoanalytic understanding of the human subject (the subject of the transference and the unconscious) to another object of understanding. When analysts write of social phenomena, they must recognize that analogies are useful only when differences are acknowledged, and an analyst's hypotheses about such phenomena must be checked against the findings of other social scientists. With this caveat, however, we can venture some hypotheses regarding the possible causes of the Chiapas events.

One way in which psychoanalysis might be able to offer some insight into these events is through its understanding of the human subject's self-division. No psychoanalyst can be surprised by the self-divisions and self-contradictions of any phenomena. This is the result not of some Hegelian reflex but rather of a practice that has as its object the human subject. Everyone is the subject of a splitting that is difficult to tolerate and even to admit.

The immediate defense against this splitting is to deny it and to act as if the division were not where it is—i.e., to act as though the split were not constitutive of the human subject as such but rather were capable of being surmounted by a unified agency of synthesis and control. From this denial results a discourse full of gaps, which both conceal the split and at the same time offer the possibility for recognizing it. This is the discourse of the ego, official discourse, which can be sustained for long periods, until something unexpected passes through it and attains the light of day. Such an event is experienced as a trauma; it is the return of the repressed, the sudden eruption of symptoms.

The traumatic events of the Chiapas can be seen as the return of a repressed division in Mexico that can be traced back to the trauma of the conquest almost 500 years ago, a trauma that could not be reabsorbed by a unified discourse and that consequently resulted in a never-ending ethnocide that has been continuously denied.

There is a method by which the subject subtracts him- or herself from the process of symbolic exchange that is the result of a decision, a choice. It is something that permits a type of experimental connection with jouissance and that produces a short circuit in relation to the Other and the Other's desire. It is a path that offers the subject a certain guidance, a more or less regulated production of separation from the effects of alienation produced by the signifier. This separation can be complete; that is, it can be an absolute refusal of the alienation produced by the signifier. It is no less paradoxical that this method is put at the disposal of the subject precisely by this Other that the subject claims to separate from. In fact, this separation is a product of industry, something that is trafficked, something that is proposed and offered by the Other in commerce, which can satisfy the demand for a radical separation and an annihilation of the “I think” in favor of an un-attenuated “I am” that is beyond all thought. As you can probably tell, I am referring to drugs and their permanent effect on the subject — namely, toxicomania, or drug addiction.

To detach oneself from the Other, from its demand, from the reconciliation of desires, is an operation that can be realized noisily through a suicidal act, which is the most radical way of slamming the door on the Other. What is produced in this instance is paradoxically an ineffaceable inscription that goes under the pretext of “no longer wanting to know anything about” the conditioning of life, and the pretext of a categorical aspiration to efface the subject in the signifying chain. This is because the act of suicide, despite the appearances of withdrawing, entails a ferocious and unrelenting contestation of the Other and its jouissance. Suicide kills; it is a “timid homicide” according to the suicide note of Caesar Pavese. He does not say; instead it throws its body like a signifier. Its tacit proposition is, “Here, these are my remains (corpse).” This is a determination that far from giving to the Other the object (a) of the subject's body in the form of a waste product, rather marks this Other in writing on it the scar of its inconsistency. It is in this sense that the rotting flesh inscribes itself in an indelible manner as the signifier of the lack in the Other, S(A), precisely when there is nothing left but (“the rest is”) silence. In effacing from itself the life of the body, it is the Other of the Law that the subject erases. Hence the fascination, horror, and repulsion, the secular condemnation and the eternal (if this were possible) fault that people try to impose on the act and agent of suicide.

A few years ago nothing would have seemed more natural to a white western-educated “liberal humanist” and a believer in psychoanalysis like myself than to make direct use of concepts and terms from psychoanalysis to investigate the post-colonial condition and discourse. But today, nothing seems less straightforward. Not only have recent cultural and post-colonial theories brought to the fore culturally-determined biases, but the contradictory and ambivalent response to psychoanalysis within post-colonial discourse merits consideration in and of itself. It is striking to note, for example, the complete absence of explicit psychoanalytic criticism in the recent Post-Colonial Studies Reader, edited by Bill Ashcroft, Gareth Griffiths, and Helen Tiffin, and this despite the extensive use made of psychoanalysis in the writings of some post-colonial thinkers, notably Homi Bhabha. In this reader, an exhaustive selection of texts on post-colonialism, not only does psychoanalysis not enjoy a section, but there are only two references in the index to Freud, none to Lacan, and none to psychoanalysis in general or to any specific psychoanalytic concept (and the same is true for the same editors' earlier The Empire Writes Back).

In this brief paper I wish to offer a hypothesis regarding the absence of psychoanalytic theory from a large component of post-colonial discourse as illustrated by the above example: the inherent privileging by psychoanalysis of fantasy over reality and repression over oppression both as a cause for human suffering and as a crucial constituent in the development of subjectivity, when translated from the realm of the individual to that of the collective, is in direct contrast to a political, specifically post-colonial, conception of center-margin relations and the formation of a political/national subject, and may thus be seen as a factor in the repulsion of psychoanalysis by a majority of post-colonial theorists. This dichotomy notwithstanding, the absence of explicit reference to psychoanalytic discourse in the Post-Colonial Studies Reader (and this despite an in-depth discussion of Homi Bhabha's position [see Parry 40-44]) seems more than a simple rejection or even oversight; I would go so far as to say that it is a projection onto psychoanalysis of the role of the voiceless “Other,” as experienced by the post-colonial. Finally, I will also try to suggest how the controversial place occupied by V. S. Naipaul between post-colonialism and the West reflects the problematic relationship between the two discourses.

But when a hero dies he doesn't die: For that hero is reborn in a Nation.

—Ernesto Cardenal, “Zero Hour”

He had them entombed in the national pantheon with magnificent pomp and all on the same level because a nation without heroes is a house without doors.

—Gabriel Garcia Marquez, The Autumn of the Patriarch

In recent years, the concept of “nation” has come under attack in US academic discussions, giving way to more fluid spatial and epistemological designations such as “borderland.” Gloria Anzaldúa, for example, argues for a border culture of the atravesados, “those who cross over, pass over, or go through the confines of the ‘normal’” (3) and destabilize the rigid definitions of borders. A destabilization of boundaries, whether in terms of the subject or of a country, challenges the exclusionary tendencies that are part of traditional forms of nation formation. Anzaldua is among many critics who have disrupted national models of literary and cultural study and helped bring into the discussion new voices from different communities around the world.1 While academia should continue to collapse disciplinary borders and engage transnational issues, political realities also demand a continuing engagement with the desire for national unity.2 As a unifying political category, the idea of nation continues to capture the imagination of many groups around the world.

If anything, the end of the Cold War has prompted a heightened desire for founding nation-states and an increased use of the “nation” banner to form coalitions. Longings for nation have manifested themselves in many different scenarios, from the horrors of Bosnia to the sometimes comical tactics of the group Queer Nation, which challenges a homogeneous concept of sexuality and the belief that the United States is made up solely of heterosexual couples. Among the former republics of the Soviet Union, the desire for independence has prompted in some cases peaceful, if problematic, transitions to nation-states. And in the United States, recent anti-immigrant fervor is based on a concept of the nation as a static geographical entity that must regulate its borders or, as some of the rhetoric would have it, protect itself from foreign intruders. “Nation” is not going away as a political category despite academic critiques of its repressive tendencies. The challenge for the future is to draw on analyses of how nation is constructed to inform the more urgent question: how to “nation”? A consideration of effective ways to transform the affinity with nation into a strategy for liberation would serve as a bridge between theoretical debates and a praxis that is sometimes forgotten or purposely evaded.

The concept of “race” has received considerable attention in recent years, both as a conceptual category and in its historical development. In both these respects, difficulties arise that might lead to some surprising connections between “race” and psychoanalysis.

As a concept, “race” designates an obscure and contested domain, seeming to refer to both natural and cultural aspects of human identity. In certain contexts, the term “race” has a strictly biological sense (and one can endorse or denounce such usage), but it can also designate a group identity that is based on a common cultural and historical inheritance. Although some writers simply take one of these senses for granted, ignoring or dismissing the other, many accounts of “race” employ the word in all its ambiguity, without distinguishing these two registers of meaning. In such cases, the term “race” is used to designate a cultural inheritance, while also referring to features that are not entirely social and that cannot be acquired by education and upbringing, such as skin color and “ancestry” in a biological sense. Discussions of the term “race” often lead back to this ambiguity, and thus to a single, decisive question concerning its status as a biological or social category.

In recent years (indeed for the last century, as Carl Degler has shown), appeals to “race” as a biological concept have been subject to strenuous criticism, not only because of the history that has bound scientific definitions of “race” to eugenics, colonialism, and the holocaust, but also because the biological definitions of “race” have not been sustained even on purely scientific grounds. The most popular and common markers of racial difference (skin color, hair, and facial features) are also the most superficial from an evolutionary point of view, in the sense that they are “surface” phenomena, which lead to classifications that do not correspond to the divisions of the human population produced by the international genetic maps which have been constructed in recent years. Even apart from this difficulty, differences in skin pigmentation remain problematic from a biological perspective: although they are commonly attributed to exposure to the sun over many generations, such explanations have not proved satisfactory to the scientific community. Variation in human skin color thus continues to escape arguments based on adaptation to the environment, posing a problem for accounts that rely on the theory of natural selection (arguments must turn to “sexual selection” as a supplementary mechanism). Likewise, the diversity of the human blood pool remains notoriously problematic from a biological standpoint, and variations in the antigens of the human immune-system (which is based on blood as well as bone marrow) are similarly obscure, though knowledge of such differences is crucial for organ transplants and other medical reasons. It is therefore not only for political and ethical reasons, but also for reasons internal to science, that the biological category of race remains problematic.

I have just returned from Bulgaria, where there are now about a hundred people actively involved in psychoanalytic studies of one kind or another. They center on the New Bulgarian University, which had regular Psychoanalytic Week events in the early 1990s, inspired and directed by David Reason of the Kent Centre for Psychoanalytic Studies. For some unaccountable reason these have ceased, but the main person at the Sofia end, Toma Tomov, has recently been appointed head of the Department of Psychiatry in the Medical School of Sofia, and he is actively involved in introducing psychoanalytic and psychodynamic thinking into the Bulgarian psychiatric community. Several joint programs are in the planning stage with the Centre for Psychotherapeutic Studies at Sheffield University in England. These include training for psychotherapists and distance learning programs in Psychoanalytic Studies; Disability Studies; Psychiatry, Philosophy, and Society; and Psychosocial Interventions in Severe Mental Disorders.

The New Bulgarian University is also in the process of setting up an Institute of Human Relations, based on psychoanalytic approaches to all levels of human interaction. It recently held a five-day Group Relations Conference, which was very interesting indeed. Thirty-six members took part in small group, large group, institutional, and consultation events which were set up to enable the participants to reflect on their own group process. One of the main themes was how unaccustomed they were to trust groups and institutions at all, even when run by people they had reason to trust. The conference had consultants from London: David Armstrong of the Tavistock Centre Consultancy Service, Gordon Lawrence of Cranefield University, and me. The Bulgarian consultants were Zlaka Mihova, Kimon Ganev, and Toma Tomov. All of these people had been involved in an earlier two-day Group Relations held at the Centre for Culture in 1992. The one this year was held in a building which, under the communist regime, had been used to indoctrinate party workers and state officials. As a result of this conference and related activities, it has been decided to set up an email forum, a web site, and an electronic journal under the title Human Relations, Authority and Justice: Experiences and Critique. These are in the process of being set up as I write. Various writings about group, institutional, and cultural dynamics, as well as work with minority groups (Gypsies are an oppressed minority in Bulgaria) will be placed on the site. The Puerto Rican Ghetto's Surlime Hystories

Anna is a young woman who suffers from “attacks.” She says that she has “bad nerves.” Everything seems to have started when she was nineteen years old and ran away from her mountain hometown, rebelling against her mother as the result of a violent fight with her sister. She was found some days later wandering naked in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The police took her to a hospital where she was admitted screaming and hitting. Her eyes were rolling, foam was coming out of her mouth, and her whole body was shaking in a seizure. Shortly thereafter, she lost consciousness. Anna was diagnosed as suffering from the Puerto Rican Syndrome (see Comas-Dias).

It was during the 1950s that the commonly noted ataque (attack) started to be identified by Anglo doctors as the Puerto Rican Syndrome. Army psychiatrists noted that Puerto Ricans in military settings behaved in “peculiar” ways whenever they were anxious. The Puerto Rican Syndrome was described as a complex of capricious somatic manifestations, combined with terror, agitation, and violence—all manifestations considered to be of psychogenic origin (see Mehlman; Fernandez-Marina; and Sierra and Trent).

The “conversion disorder” known as ataque coincides point by point with the Charcotian and Freudian description of hysterical conversion, which includes anesthesia, hyperesthesia, pain, paralysis, convulsions, hyperventilation, mutism, uncommunicativeness, self-mutilations, violence, and in some cases deafness and blindness. In Studies in Hysteria (see Lacan, Seminar V). Freud identifies as a hystericizing situation one in which too much time is spent taking care of a sick person, placing one in a passive situation, awaiting the other's demand. This is a position in which one's own wishes remain in suspense, repressed, subordinated, servicing the other's needs. Any attempt to have an independent wish is suppressed and returned as guilt. Today, Puerto Ricans repeat this hysterical position of subaltern service occupied by Freud's Viennese hysterics a century ago (see Garrison).1

Lacan, Politics, Aesthetics, edited by Willy Apollon and Richard Feldstein, is an anthology of recent work by Willy Apollon, Elizabeth J. Bellamy, Danielle Bergeron, Hanjo Berressem, Elizabeth Bronfen, Lucie Cantin, Richard Feldstein, Bruce Fink, Maire Jaanus, Juliet Flower MacCannell, Catherine Portugues, Ellie Ragland, Judith Roof, Peter Widmer, and Slavoj Žižek.

Their essays represent what Feldstein calls a “second phase” of Lacanian studies, ushered in by the groundbreaking work of Slavoj Žižek and Juliet Flower MacCannell in the field of cultural studies. Although Feldstein credits MacCannell and Žižek primarily with applying Lacan's theories to questions of race, gender, and class, their influence is apparent in this collection less in the thematic concerns of its authors than in their preoccupation with the jouissance at stake in political discourse, and its consequences for the positioning of the subject in the aftermath of the Enlightenment. Against the apparent reversibility of legislative “equality,” psychoanalysis insists upon the fundamental disproportion between the subject's jouissance and the law that pretends to uphold it, the phallic signifier that represents all subjects “equally,” and thus inadequately. The particular focus of Lacan, Politics, Aesthetics, as the title suggests, is the interplay between politics and aesthetics, or the role of representation in upholding the authority of the signifier and denying or filling the lack in the Other.

Willy Apollon's dense introduction frames the theoretical stakes of the collection by positing that “politics makes a promise it cannot keep.” In spite of its stated dedication to the “pursuit of happiness,” the post-Enlightenment discourse of liberalism is incapable of responding to the subject's particular relation to jouissance. In the negotiation between the “common good” and personal satisfaction or private ownership, “liberal discourse would have us believe that there is a gap capable of being improved upon, not an insurmountable contradiction” (xxii).

Some ninety-odd years since its publication, Daniel Paul Schreber's Denkwürdigkeiten eines Nervenkranken continues to sustain a thriving cottage industry in Schreber studies—far less developed perhaps than the critical industries spawned by the work of Joyce, Kafka, or Pynchon, but no less likely to subject its participants to the effects of a certain preprogramming (as Freud himself discovered early on).1 In a sense, however, the Schreber industry has thrived precisely because its practitioners have refused to take Schreber at his word: either because they have tended to reduce his megalomaniacal fantasies to the status of simple by-products of Oedipal conflict (with Moritz Schreber, Paul Flechsig, or God Himself), or because they have passed over the detail of Schreber's cosmological scheme in their rush to read the despotism of the Schreberian father as proto-fascistic, as the coming Nazism writ small.

In this extraordinarily rewarding new book, Eric Santner suggests that taking Schreber seriously means learning to appreciate Schreber's sense for the dirty little secret of symbolic power—its dependence upon forms of “tautological nonsense” (e.g., “The law is the law”), the idiotic repetition of which serves to obscure the fact that such power is “without ultimate justification or legitimation” (10-11,43). What Schreber's cosmological delusions reveal, in other words, is “the inner ‘rottenness’ of every symbolic investiture insofar as it remains dependent on a dimension of performative force, compulsion, drive”—a dimension that Santner clearly equates with “enjoyment,” jouissance (37,95). To take Schreber seriously, in short, is to reread the Memoirs at the point of intersection of several powerful theoretical optics: Benjamin's work on violence as the “something rotten in law,” Bourdieu's uncovering of a “performative magic” inherent to all acts of symbolic investiture, and Žižek's insistence upon an obscene enjoyment necessarily secreted by symbolic power and authority (9-11, 52).

Charles Melman has recently pointed out the long-lasting consequences of the social trauma embodied in the colonization of Brazil by the Portuguese (Melman 93).1 One of these consequences, strongly associated with the violence involved in the annihilation of the native cultures, is a difficulty in the implementation of the function of the symbolic father, which results in problems concerning agreed-upon rules and procedures, something that affects the organization of social relationships as a whole.

The lack of a firmly established symbolic lather-function in this type of society would seem to generate a strong demand for a real father to appear and solve all the problems. It has been argued that one consequence of this demand is the tendency to welcome dictatorships in Brazilian political life (see Teixeira 51).

It would also appear that this psychological structure would affect not only members of the native cultures but also members of the Portuguese culture, who in such a structure would be in a subjective position vulnerable to the unlimited jouissance that assails subjects who have inadequate anchoring points in the symbolic order. Paulo Freire, in Pedagogy of the Oppressed, has described with great accuracy how an oppressed people develops an identification with the oppressor. As a result of such identification, this proximity with unlimited jouissance became a model for the whole society, as can be seen in a character like Vadinho in Jorge Amado's novel, Dona Flor e Seus Dois Maridos. Vadinho, who represents in many respects the ideal Brazilian (he doesn't work, has many women, plays cards every evening, and is very good at sex) dies on the last day of Carnival, in the middle of an orgasm.

With the arrival of the African slaves, the situation became even more complex. The slaves, in becoming part of the production system, supported the possibility of unlimited jouissance for the Portuguese. On the other hand, they also became a source of symbolic references: living on farms, but forming communities of up to a hundred members (something that did not happen in the United States, where the farms required a much smaller number of slaves), they succeeded in maintaining their traditions.

So much appeals to me in the pedagogical approach Jeff Berman delineates in his book Diaries to an English Professor that I was delighted to see his further discussion of introspective diary writing in your Spring 1996 issue. Since I began using Berman's teaching approach—which is consistent with my own philosophies of self-reflective thinking leading to personal growth—in my classrooms starting in January of this past year, there are several points in Berman's article that I would like to highlight in relation to my own teaching experiences. First and foremost, I wholeheartedly agree that introspective diary writing can successfully be used in courses where literature and psychoanalysis are not the focus. My incorporation of Berman's teaching approach has adapted his methodology to the setting of a composition classroom. I maintain, of course, the same crucial safeguards: diaries are confidential, they are ungraded, they may be written on any topic ranging from self-disclosure to ideas for formal essays, and my return comments are neither judgmental nor psychoanalytically prescriptive, but rather an act of responding with objective em-pathy. I do select several diaries to read each week, and the act of selection becomes a self-reflective exercise as to why I am selecting the specific diaries to which I am drawn.

Often, and this is certainly true early on in the semester, it is the students who determine which diaries are read, since they must plainly note on the face of their diaries when I am not to read their entry for the week. As the semester progresses, and true to Berman's experiences as well, fewer and fewer of my students declined permission to read their writing out loud. In many instances, after several weeks of reading diaries out loud, specific students were requesting that I read their diaries out loud, arguing for reasons why their entry should be selected, and often highlighting their request with transparent-ink markers or different colored pens. I read these “requests” appended to the diary entry to the class as well. In the larger cultural arena beyond the classroom, I like to think about these “requests” as pleas to be heard, and reading the diaries out loud functions as fulfillment for those pleas and, for the student, as the commencement of gaining a “voice” that can make a difference in society.

The human race has found its destiny in self-destruction.

—Findley 98

The hatred of the Other is the hatred of our own excess of enjoyment.

—Žižek, Tarrying 206

In their effort to diminish the structural rigidity of Althusserian Marxism and the humanist legacies of cultural materialism, theorists of “radical democracy,” such as Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe, have repeatedly declared that society—understood as the harmonious coexistence of diverse individuals and groups—is “impossible” (Hegemony 112, 122, 143, 156; New Reflections 91-92). Laclau and Mouffe's theory of “the impossibility of society” circumvents various problems in Marx and Engels's “organic utilitarian” model (Gewirth 10-11), which aims to render happiness the psychic result of social harmony and class equanimity. In part three of The German Ideology (1846), for instance, Marx and Engels argued:

Only in community with others has each individual the means of cultivating his gifts in all directions; only in the community, therefore, is personal freedom possible…. [Within] the illusory community, in which individuals have up till now combined, … [the] right to the undisturbed enjoyment, upon certain conditions, of fortuity and chance has … been called personal freedom …. With the community of revolutionary proletarians on the other hand, who take their conditions of existence and those of all members of society under their control, it is just the reverse; it is as individuals that the individuals participate in it. It is just this combination of individuals (assuming the advanced stage of modern productive forces, of course) which puts the conditions of the free development and movement of individuals under their control. (74-75)1

Noting this model's reliance on illusory notions of national harmony,2 and its limited account of group relations, Laclau and Mouffe produced a model of “radical democracy” that avoids many of Marx and Engels's conceptual blindspots (Hegemony 23, 26-27).3 In place of Marx and Engels's assumptions of future harmony, they stress that society's impossibility is ultimately to our advantage: its lack of closure makes possible political change (for a related argument, see Althusser 32, 58). At the same time, Laclau and Mouffe's work has contributed to a celebratory emphasis on contingency in political theory, and on displacement and hybridity in postcolonial theory, whose advocates often propose that a multiplicity of subject positions and their corresponding forms of alienation can determine political strategy (see Mouffe, Return 20, 70).

We all love to instruct, though we can teach only what is not worth knowing.

—Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice (281)

As professors we love to instruct, yet despite or perhaps because of the mounds of lecture material we convey to our students, the lengthy bibliographies we assign them to read, and the formal essays we ask them to write, we may gradually become disillusioned by how little real learning occurs in the classroom. By real learning I mean the ability to translate abstract theory into meaningful personal knowledge. We live in a highly theoretical age in which, all too often, the personal element of learning is ignored, resulting in teaching that is increasingly abstract, impersonal, and academic. We may theorize the personal, but rarely do we become personal in our discussions of literature or life. This problem seems especially acute in psychoanalytic literary criticism, where, in an effort to show how complex theories deriving from Freud, Lacan, or Derrida may be applied to literature, we lose sight of the real people who sit in our classrooms, whose everyday experiences seem worlds apart from those of master theorists.

For many years I have been trying to find ways to encourage my students to personalize psychoanalytic theory to order to increase their understanding of themselves and their world. The method of teaching I have found most rewarding involves the use of non-graded introspective diaries. Beginning in 1976, when I created and taught the first course in psychoanalytic literary criticism at the University at Albany, I have asked my students to keep a weekly diary in which they apply psychoanalytic theory to their own lives. In outlining the course, I told my students that just as we would use our class discussions to analyze fictional characters' dreams, desires, fantasies, and defenses, so would the students be encouraged to turn their attention inward and, with the help of insights acquired through readings and class discussions, engage in self-analysis. The diaries, then, would become the “laboratory” part of the course, allowing students to pursue the Delphic Oracle's injunction, “Know thyself.

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels   Received his doctorate in psychoanalysis from the University of Paris VIII. Recently, we have witnessed an emergence on television of a form of discourse that appears to approach many of the desired aims of both psychoanalysis and liberalism. Of course, I am talking about talk shows and their dedication to the establishment of public spaces for the airing of private issues in a democratic setting of free speech. What one finds on talk shows is an open discussion of some of the most repressed and essential subjects of modern American culture: drug abuse, domestic violence, changing gender roles, the breakup of the nuclear family, and so on. This open form of discourse counters the Left's criticism that television only presents upper- and middle-class heterosexual men and women who suffer from none of the major problems that plague our society.1 Talk shows often concentrate on the lower strata of the socio-economic ladder, and they rarely shy away from any type of controversial social problem. In thus rendering visible neglected aspects of American culture, these programs could be said to perform a valuable social function.

But are these programs liberating, or do they participate in what Foucault has called a “disciplining of the soul?”2 In other words, when citizens are encouraged to talk in a public forum about what appear to be their most intimate desires and experiences, are they not being pushed toward an alienating discourse that simply extends the reach of dominant ideologies further into their private lives? More specifically, does not this form of social discourse contribute to the production of a perverse culture where subjects are forced to submit all of their sexual desires to a rigid set of rules and scenarios?

Lacan's theory of perversion can help explain both why people go on these shows and why people watch them. For Lacan, the central feature of all perversions is the attempt to force sexual enjoyment into the intersubjective field of the symbolic Other.3 While perverse activities appear to be based on a desire to transgress the social order, what we actually find in them are constant attempts to create a law of enjoyment. Common to perverse activities is a proliferation of symbolic stereotypes, contracts, role-playing, uniforms, and gender formations. In these perverse scenarios, the social symbolization of gender roles is performed and erotized.
