America's half a million foster children are the responsibility of all and a worry to all who care about the upcoming generation. Foster children are excessively represented among older children who populate special education classes, homeless shelters, jails, and mental health facilities. As adolescents, many foster children soon begin making new generations of foster children. Foster children are recipients of often quite belated and costly treatment for deeply ingrained mental disorders that are greatly aggravated by multiple transfers among foster homes. It therefore makes good clinical, social, and economic sense to try to prevent the aggravating influence of unstable placements in this pathology-prone population.

I have long been interested in applications of psychoanalytic theory and technique to preventive interventions with children (see Kliman, “Nursery,” “Cornerstone,” “Preventive,” “Summary,” and “Breakthrough”). I have been especially interested in preventing the effects of severe traumas by enhancing the personal narrative and related sublimative activities of young children (see Aust; Klagsbrun and Kliman; Kliman, “Nursery”; Kliman and Rosenfeld; Lopez and Kliman, “Mommy” and “Cornerstone”; Stein and Kliman; Kliman, Oklan and Wolfe). Systematic preventive interventions with foster children have increasingly been my focus (see Kliman, “Summary” and “Breakthrough”). In designing an intervention program for foster children, I hypothesized that the adversities preceding being placed in foster care involved a frequently traumatic set of stresses whose pathological social consequences could be the target of the preventive intervention. These prior adversities include relationship deficiency, relationship toxicity, and relationship discontinuity stresses: neglect, abuse, rejection, and ultimately the loss of family relationships.

Editor's Column

Lacan's “Civilization and its Discontents”

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher  

A casual glance at the title of the lead article in this issue, Lacan's previously untranslated paper on psychoanalysis and criminology, might leave one with the impression that this is a rather narrowly focused piece likely to be of interest only to criminologists. In fact, however, Lacan's paper might well be titled “Civilization and Its Discontents,” for it functions to clarify, elaborate, or critique many of the formulations of Freud's book concerning the most fundamental psychological consequences of civilization, as well as the psychological roots of the most serious problems facing civilization. Crime, as a manifestation of the most severe discontent with civilization, serves Lacan as the royal road to what we might call the social unconscious. “The reality of the criminal,” Lacan says, “indicates the fundamental social province of psychoanalysis” (19).

Lacan's paper makes three general points concerning the relation of psychoanalysis to culture and society:

Psychoanalytic discoveries provide the basis for a general model of subjectivity that can help us understand both the psychological roots of social and cultural phenomena—that is, the motives that cause humans to produce these phenomena—and the basic psychological consequences that social and cultural formations can have.

Psychoanalysis offers us a method for investigating the specific psychological roots or consequences of a specific social or cultural phenomenon.

Psychoanalysis offers us a technique for intervening in social problems through addressing their psychological roots or consequences.

In my comments here, I want to focus on the first of these points, and specifically on how, according to Lacan, psychoanalysis can help us understand and intervene in the problem that Freud described as the most serious concern facing civilization: human aggression.

Psychoanalysis as a General Model of Subjectivity

Richard Boothby

Richard Boothby

If Freud's discovery of the unconscious has taught us to discern what lies hidden under the carpet of consciousness, it has done so in no small part by renewing our astonishment at human behavior that is immediately observable. It is in that spirit that, midway through the text of Totem and Taboo, Freud quotes a description of a fourth century Bedouin ritual of sacrifice. For Freud, as for Willliam Robertson Smith, from whom Freud borrows a record of the ritual, the very strangeness of the event it describes, the measured solemnity of ceremony followed by a frenzy of shocking violence, presents a powerful challenge for explanation:

The victim of the sacrifice, a camel, ‘is bound upon a rude altar of stones piled together, and when the leader of the band has thrice led the worshippers round the altar in a solemn procession accompanied with chants, he inflicts the first wound … and in all haste drinks of the blood that gushes forth. Forthwith the whole company fall on the victim with their swords, hacking off pieces of the quivering flesh and devouring them raw with such wild haste, that in the short interval between the rise of the day star which marked the hour for the service to begin, and the disappearance of its rays before the rising sun, the entire camel, body and bones, skin, blood and entrails, is wholly devoured.’ (Freud 138).

Already in this picture of ecstatic savagery, itself a kind of primal scene, we are brought up short before one of the central mysteries explored by psychoanalysis, that in which an elemental fulguration of desire is released amid spectacular violence. We are confronted, that is, with the enigma of what Jacques Lacan has called “jouissance.” Equally remarkable is the fact that this eruption of violent excess is so elaborately staged in the architecture of a ritual. As a carefully orchestrated, collective murder followed by a feast on the body of the victim, the Bedouin sacrifice recalls for Freud the primal patricide from which all manner of cultural forms arise and take shape. “The totem meal,” he concludes, “which is perhaps mankind's earliest festival, would thus be a repetition and a commemoration of this memorable and criminal deed, which was the beginning of so many things—of social organization, of moral restrictions and of religion” (Freud 142). Yet what is most challenging about the Bedouin killing-feast is that it is less the exception than the rule for many ancient or aboriginal cultures. In a similar rite among the African Dinka recounted by Godfrey Lienhardt, a cow is tied to a stake and surrounded by a chanting throng whose members take turns hurling insults at the beast and raining blows down upon it. In a climactic rush, the animal is trampled and crushed by a stampede of the young men of the tribe, after which the carcass is carved and eaten. Elaborate sacrificial rites are familiar to us from classical Greece and Rome and were central to Vedic Hindu traditions; indeed the word vedi designates the site of the sacrificial altar. The Hindu rites included vegetative sacrifices, in which stalks of the soma plant were cut and ground up, but the linkage to earlier animal and even human sacrifice is made clear by the use in both instances of the verb hanti: “to slay” or “kill.” Bears were a special object of sacrifice among both the Ouataouak tribe in North American and the Aino of Japan, as were dogs among the Iroquois and African Minyanka, sheep among the Zulu, Thonga, and Lovedu, and black oxen among the Swazis (de Hersh 195). Despite Islamic injunctions against blood sacrifice, the ritual slaughter of sheep, goats, and camels continues in such quantity among pilgrims to Mt. Arafat that Saudi authorities have used bulldozers to remove the carcasses (Burkert 11).

Richard Rorty provides a striking example of a certain popular, optimistic, and poststructuralist view of language when he endorses Katherine MacKinnon's call for a change in male attitudes toward rape. This change requires, Rorty points out, that “people … feel … revulsion and rage where they once felt indifference or resignation” (44). What must be generated here is a new emotional response. Rorty argues this new response can be produced by language, through what MacKinnon terms an “extension of logical space” (44). If social injustice is perpetuated by thoughtless and unreflective habits of thought, and if social justice is impeded by an acceptance of or indifference to such habits of injustice, new language, producing new “logical space” and emotional response, can lead people to no longer tolerate what they once unthinkingly accepted. Rorty explains:

One way to change instinctive emotional reactions is to provide new language that will facilitate new reactions. By “new language” I mean not just new words but also creative misuses of language—familiar words used in ways that initially sound crazy. Something traditionally regarded as a moral abomination can become an object of general satisfaction, or conversely, as a result of the increased popularity of an alternative description of what is happening. Such popularity extends logical space by making descriptions of situations that used to seem crazy seem sane. (44)

Rorty's goal is to “change instinctive emotional reactions.” And Rorty's plan for this change is to adopt “creative misuses of language.” “Instinctive emotional reactions” normally imply spontaneous emotive impulses that precede language use. Rorty's argument, however, suggests the opposite: language use generates instinctive response. This paper will take a Lacanian perspective to explore how “instinctive” reactions are interwoven with language—both produced by and resisted by linguistic structure.

Rorty's hope that “logical space” can be “extended” by “creative misuses” of language reflects important poststructuralist assumptions about the nature of language and subjectivity. Because reality is at least in part constructed by language, and because subjects (and their instinctive responses), also, are “interpellated” or brought into existence by discourse, new discourse performances can be imagined as effective mechanisms for the formulation of new modes of subjectivity and social reality. New uses of language, poststructuralism argues, can produce new instinctive responses.

Susan Schwartz   Recently completed her doctorate at the University of Melbourne. In his short polemic, “The Politics of Subjectivity,” Terry Eagleton laments the absence of a theory of the subject that can provide the control, organization, and direction required by a fundamental political transformation such as Revolution (48). For Eagleton, such a theory would grasp “social transformation as at once diffusion and affirmation, the death and the birth of the subject” (48). He is explicit in his understanding—or misunderstanding—that the splitting of the subject precludes the possibility of concerted political action. Eagleton does not explore the primary effect of that splitting—namely, the creation of the subject as desiring and the consequent emergence of agency on the basis of this desire. Instead, Eagleton sees desire as coterminous with the diffusion of the subject and thus as an impediment to the subject's pursuing a coherent political goal.

I shall argue, in contrast, that far from being in opposition to agency, desire is its very ground. Furthermore, I will demonstrate that identification, a process fundamental to political action, is both a cause and an effect of desire. Through an examination of The Words to Say It, an autobiographical fiction by French-Algerian writer Marie Cardinal, and the revolutionary writings of Frantz Fanon, I will explore the relations among desire, identification, and political action in the constitution of the revolutionary subject. In so doing, I will draw a distinction between the subject produced within a psychoanalytic discourse and the subject constituted within the master discourses of Revolution and Colonization.

In the colonized subject, the intra-psychic antagonism produced by social antagonism is particularly evident, and it is this intersection of the psychic and the social that Eagleton's formulation does not address. It is a significant omission. The subject formed within a condition of antagonism experiences a radical disjunction between his sense of who he is— his identity—and the subject position into which he is interpellated. This disjunction constitutes an intra-psychic conflict or antagonism in the subject, and this conflict is experienced as a lack that is present even if the subject behaves with a unity of purpose that masks that lack. Now, unity of purpose is the product of fantasy, which arises in response to the lack. As Henry Krips observes, “social antagonisms may function as crucibles for the constitution of desires by acting as sites at which subjects repeat their primal lack” (59). A parallel can be drawn, he argues, between social antagonism (as defined by Laclau and Mouffe) and Lacan's interpretation of the fort-da game as emblematic of the primal scene of lack. Even though the experience of primal lack is repressed, individuals continue to repeat their original lack throughout their lives “by engaging in games of pursuit, the repetitive absencing and bringing back to presence of objects over which they have some degree of control” (67).1 Although the lack can never be filled, the absence of satisfaction is not disabling for the subject; on the contrary, it produces the subject as agent by eliciting fantasy. Fantasy gives the subject the consistency it lacks by locating an object that promises to fill his lack and, at the same time, channeling desire in the direction of realizing this object. At this point desire and fantasy, identification and agency intersect, for desire and fantasy are both cause and effect of the process of identification that gives the subject his sense of unity.2 As a consequence, fantasy is preliminary to and prerequisite for political action, for it is both the support of the revolutionary subject's desire and the medium within which social transformation is imagined.

A technical language should never be developed when the words of ordinary language will do. If a theory produces its own peculiar vocabulary, this is only justified if the new terms are attended by new meanings and concepts, or if they clarify matters that are left obscure by the available stock of words. Thus, if the role played by a new term can be performed by a word already in circulation, critics are justified in dismissing the new vocabulary as “jargon.”

When the term “deconstruction,” for example, is taken as a verb and used as the equivalent of “to criticize,” or “to analyze,” or even simply “to discuss,” critics may rightly claim that the verbal innovation only repeats familiar ideas under the guise of novelty (“Isn't deconstruction really just close reading?”).

The well known communist joke inquires: “What is the difference between an optimist and a pessimist in the Soviet Union?” “A pessimist thinks that everything is so bad that it can't get worse, while an optimist thinks that it can.” Nowadays, many Russians and other East-Europeans still hold such an “optimistic” view, since they are confronted with the economic chaos of early capitalism, which makes their lives even more difficult than it was under the communist regime. Some of the people thus feel deep despair and daydream about those lost times of less freedom but more social security.1 For such nostalgic people, the fall of the communist regime was the event that caused the disarray of their lives. Clinging to this perception, they act like the hysterics who always find a point in their symbolic economy, a particular event, that instigated their suffering. Such a hysteric usually concludes: “If only my mother hadn't done this in my youth …, if only that encounter had never occurred …, if only I could turn back the clock and arrange things to develop differently.” The belief in such an “if only” is a necessary fantasy that enables the hysteric to sustain the position of a suffering innocent victim. Since the clock cannot be turned back, the hysterics can do nothing to change the situation.

Those who are nostalgic about the communist past act in a similar fashion when they grumble and pine for the former times: since these times are forever gone, they do not need to act to improve their current situation. That is why the vast majority of these people do not engage in a serious political struggle; they do not organize political parties which would, for example, fight for the return of communism. Instead, they persist in the comfortable position of the lamenting victim.2 The paradox is that in the past, they wished communism to end, but they did not truly believe that their wish could be fulfilled. And today they act in a similar fashion when they dream about returning to the safe shelter of the communist institutions, while knowing that this cannot happen. Contemporary Romania presents a model case in this regard, since it is governed by those ex-communists who now form the new capitalist elite, but whose ideology promises the reestablishment of communist welfare. But as I will try to demonstrate, this longed-for communist past bears the marks of trauma: Ceausescu and the architectural monuments of his regime.

Renata Salecl presents a historical and political analysis of the changes in East Europe through a felicitous mingling of the discourses of feminism, psychoanalysis, law, and philosophy. She thereby opens out, at this millennial moment, questions of relevance not merely to the East European countries but to the liberal democracies whose triumph over Stalinism has brought an unexpected challenge, stirring up interconnected elements of thought across disciplines. At such a moment of dangerous complacency for the West, the times before and after the collapse of Stalinism deserve our closest attention.

Salecl interposes theoretical arguments with surveys of recent history in Czechoslovakia and the former Yugoslavia. What ties the two together is the part played by fantasy in political life. Fantasy in politics is a subject that has been insufficiently explored. One reason is not far to seek: its exploitation by the Nazis has strengthened a dangerous dislike for the topic that is attributable to an Enlightenment presupposition, which still lingers tacitly in political philosophy: that rationality is best characterized by a dismissal of anything that partakes of illusion. Salecl shows that the theoretical place of fantasy has now become an urgent concern for political inquiry. What emerges from her considerations is that, if the rationalist dislike continues to encourage the ignoring of fantasy, then those who realise its potential for the attraction of power will be left to manipulate it as they please, as the East European examples she gives amply demonstrate.

What is the source of fantasy? Her answer is the Lacanian one: that it springs from the insuppressible attempts of jouissance, the libidinal, anarchic source of desire, to overcome the incompleteness of its symbolic direction. The symbolic holds out in its secret implications the prospect of an ultimate completion of all desire, a return to a non-existent maternal plenitude from which the self in process is induced to assume that it has emerged. The experience of the symbolic's unending failure, coupled with its unending promise, produces the Lacanian objet a, the fantasy of a stop-gap for that gap. Within the psyche the symbolic, under the pressure of this illusion, takes on the form of a superego that derives illicit enjoyment from the law itself. For the superego owes its unforgiving obduracy to the very puissance it is ostensibly set up to control. Although the fantasy inhabits the superego unacknowledged, it nevertheless, and all the more insidiously, demands the actual realization of the objet a.

When, a couple of years ago, the disclosure of Michael Jackson's alleged “immoral” private behavior (his sexual games with boys under age) dealt a blow to his innocent Peter Pan image elevated above sexual and race differences (or concerns), some perspicacious commentators asked the obvious question: what's all the fuss about? Wasn't this so-called “dark side of Michael Jackson” all the time here for all of us to see, in the video spots that accompanied his musical releases and that were saturated with ritualized violence and obscene sexual gestures (exemplarily in the case of Thriller and Bad)? This paradox illustrates perfectly Lacan's thesis according to which “the unconscious is outside,” not hidden in any unfathomable depths—or, to quote The X Files motto: “The truth is out there.”

Such a focusing on material externality proves very fruitful in the analysis of the inherent antagonisms of an ideological edifice. Do not the two opposed architectural designs of Casa del Fascio (the local headquarters of the Fascist party), Adolfo Coppede's neo-Imperial pastiche from 1928 and Giuseppe Teragni's highly modernist transparent glass-house from 1934-36, in their simple juxtaposition, reveal the inherent contradiction of the Fascist ideological project, which simultaneously advocates a return to pre-modern organicist corporatism and the unheard-of mobilization of all social forces in the service of rapid modernization? An even better example is provided by the great projects of public buildings in the Soviet Union of the 1930s, which put on the top of a flat multi-story office building a gigantic statue of the idealized New Man or couple. Within a couple of years, the tendency became clearly discernible to flatten even more the office building—the actual working place for the living people—so that it changed more and more into a mere pedestal for the larger-than-life statue—does this external, material feature of architectural design not render visible the “truth” of the Stalinist ideology in which actual, living people are reduced to instruments, sacrificed as the pedestal for the specter of the future New Man, an ideological monster that crushes under his feet actual living men? The paradox is that whereas anyone in the Soviet Union of the 1930s who might say openly that the vision of the Socialist New Man was an ideological monster squashing actual people would immediately be arrested—it was allowed and even encouraged to make this point via the architectural design: “the truth is out there.” What we are thus arguing is not simply that ideology permeates also the alleged extra-ideological strata of everyday life, but that this materialization of ideology in the external materiality renders visible inherent antagonisms that the explicit formulation of ideology cannot afford to acknowledge. It is as if an ideological edifice, in order to function “normally,” must obey a kind of “imp of perversity” and articulate its inherent antagonism in the externality of its material existence.

Freud and His “Negro”: Psychoanalysis as Ally and Enemy of African Americans

Claudia Tate

Claudia Tate

Claudia Tate   Professor of English at George Washington University and author of Domestic Allegories of Political Desire: The Black Heroine's Text at the Turn of the Century and Desire and the Protocols of Race: Black Novels and Psychoanalysis (forthcoming).

Freud… paid regular visits to Vienna. He went there on July 8 and returned on September 27. He took with him an American patient, whom he referred to as his “negro.” He had told us of this old joke, dating back to 1886, but curiously enough none of his children were familiar with it.

—Ernest Jones, The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud(1957)

On the face of it, psychoanalysis might seem like a weapon that humanists and social scientists of African descent would eagerly employ in their works to articulate the complex effects of racism on Americans of all origins. After all, what could be more useful in opposing racism than a practice designed to expose and undermine the deep psychological foundations of destructive attitudes and behaviors—of which racism is an exemplary instance? The fact is, though, that black scholars have not rushed to embrace psychoanalysis as an ally in their struggle against this particular psychopathology of white people. In fact, African American scholars have generally been rather hostile toward psychoanalysis.

Why is this the case? Is it simply an oversight, the result, perhaps, of a lack of familiarity on the part of many black scholars with psychoanalysis? Might it be due to their recognition that psychoanalysis, as a practice of individual psychotherapy, can never affect more than an extremely small portion of the millions of individual white racists that populate our nation and the globe? Or could the eschewing of psychoanalysis by African American scholars be the result of their recognition that psychoanalysis may not be the unambiguous ally to their cause that it would seem to be?

I believe that all three of these possibilities have some validity. It is certainly true, for instance, that psychoanalysis is and has been primarily a resource for the well-to-do and that far fewer black people than white are included in this category. And it is also the case that as a form of individual therapy, psychoanalysis offers no clear and immediate path to greater freedom and justice of the sort that at least at one time appeared to be offered by demonstrations, sit-ins, and legal battles. More important, though, are two related facts: the practitioners of psychoanalysis are almost categorically all white, and its analytical models disregard the effects of racial difference on the lived experiences of the analysts and analysands. These latter factors, I believe, constitute the main reasons African American scholars have been so hesitant in embracing psychoanalysis. For once African Americans recognize that psychoanalysis always seems to boil down to sexual matters to the exclusion of race matters, psychoanalysis appears to ally itself as much or more with the forces of white privilege than with those of racial equality.

When I was invited to speak about Lacan and postcoloniality I had a single mental and visceral response, which I can best sum up with a slightly incredulous inflection: “Post?colonial?” How hopeful, yet how unsecured that term sounds. Globalized economic systems, run down information superhighways and the “glamorous tentacles of media colonization” (Phillips 13),1 are taking to a higher power Lacan's early image for our latter-day, psychotic pseudo-patriarchy—“la grand'route—étre père.” More intent on acquiring sales than national territories, more focused on conquering corporate, and not mere human, bodies, colonialism has surely only shifted ground where the subject's alienation is concerned. The Disney version of life is about to touch us all. Yet, although its effects are visible to everyone, the way neo-colonialism subjects us remains obscure. We can look for analogies in those compelling, and uncannily familiar, depictions of colonization's psychic ravages offered by early anti-colonial writers, like Fanon and Memmi. However, recognizing that what was once a seemingly restricted human problematic is now the general case requires more analytic power, lest we risk unwittingly reinforcing colonization's most damaging features. In this paper, I explore what I call the “colonial complex.” It is both personal and political. I will describe and specify it. For me, it is an ethical disorder, a complex now ironically re-transplanted to European cultures from the very places to which it had sought to expel and export it.

In my view, if there to be any relationship at all between psychoanalysis and postcolonial analysis, the subject must be the focus: not the poststructural, dispersed subject, or not only that subject, but the classical subject in its three dimensions—as sovereign individual, citizen under law, and person before God (Teshome Gabriel's formulation). Well before poststructuralism, the “classical” subject suffered traumatic blows to these categories—it just didn't know it. Its failure of knowledge became a major component of its colonizing force. So I will amend my statement: it is the unconscious subject of colonialism that must be analyzed.

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher

Mark Bracher   Professor of English and Director of the Center for Literature and Psychoanalysis at Kent State University. Why a Journal “for the Psychoanalysis of Culture & Society”?

Psychoanalysis of Culture & Society. The very name makes people uncomfortable, anxious. It is disturbing first of all because its meaning is not immediately clear: we know what psychoanalyzing an individual involves, but what would it mean to psychoanalyze a culture or society? Does the name imply unleashing hordes (primal ones, perhaps) of pseudo-analysts to impose psychoanalysis on the unsuspecting masses? Or is the name merely the result of a category mistake, the faulty assumption that a mode of therapy designed to produce individual change could be applied to entire societies to produce social change? Why, people have asked, isn't the publication called “Journal for the Psychoanalytic Study of Culture & Society,” or simply “Journal for Psychoanalysis, Culture, & Society”?

The answer is that this journal's name, like its existence, aims to disrupt the traditional (and still current) mode of “applying” psychoanalysis, which involves producing psychoanalytic “studies” of cultural artifacts (works of literature, art, music, etc.) with little or no concern for whether such academic studies provide any benefits beyond advancing their authors' careers. JPCS and its parent organization, the Association for the Psychoanalysis of Culture & Society (APCS), are committed to an applied psychoanalysis that produces not just academic interpretations but social benefits. APCS and JPCS aim to bring psychoanalysis as both a theory and a practice to bear on social and cultural phenomena in ways that promote beneficial social change. More specifically, the association and journal are dedicated to using psychoanalysis to formulate social and cultural practices that can alter the psychological roots of socially destructive attitudes and behavior, such as racism, sexism, homophobia, and various other forms of interpersonal, intergroup, and structural violence.

The psychoanalysis in the journal's title, then, is meant to be of culture and society in the same way that democracy is of the people: a process engaged in by a. society as a whole and for the society as a whole, rather than by and for just a few privileged individuals. JPCS is dedicated to a theoretical and practical psychoanalysis that will engage with collective meanings and meaning systems (cultures) and provide benefits for human collectives (societies) rather than only for those individuals who have the social, economic, and geographic locations necessary to procure personal psychoanalytic treatment. We support a psychoanalysis that is an integral part of culture and society, functioning as a resource through which a culture can interrogate and produce its meanings and thus as a tool that a society can use to help resolve its conflicts, internal and external.

Postcolonialism and Psychoanalysis: The Example of Haiti

Willy Apollon

Willy Apollon

Willy Apollon   Holds a doctorate in philosophy from the Sorbonne and is consulting analyst at a psychoanalytic treatment center for young psychotics in Québec City. Of Haitian origin, he has been involved in the struggle to reestablish democracy in Haiti.

The question of postcolonialism is a question that the Western world asks within its own problematic of the globalization of its model of democracy. But isn't democracy one now, following the shattering collapse of the socialist model? This is the most general assumption, in the North and in the West. A certain number of nations are experimenting with some equally novel forms of government, which are being grouped under the concept of fundamentalism. I would be tempted to say, as a preface to this discussion, that what characterizes our political epoch is the demarcation between, on the one hand, the regimes that offer a determined resistance to the globalization of the Western model of democracy, by setting forth a different model of popular mobilization in the construction of the nation, and on the other hand, the regimes that either are forced to conform to the democratic model or that spontaneously seek in democracy a means of participating in the globalization of capital and of information.

This is also, in my opinion, the crux of postcolonialism today. I would express it as a particular antinomy resulting from the conflictual, or even contradictory, relations between two modern imperatives: the need for popular mobilization in the economic development of a democratic system, and the imperative for the globalization of the liberal economy, which is the paradigmatic model of the democracy in question. The question that is prohibited within this problematic, and repressed from official discourses, is that of the principal actor—or, if you prefer, of the subject of history.

The angle from which I approach these questions is informed, first and foremost, by my experience as a clinician and theoretician preoccupied with the epistemological presuppositions of a psychoanalytic practice attempting to free itself from the ethnocentrism and cultural imperialism that today dominate the theory and the practice of psychoanalysis. Second, the concrete experience of my personal engagement at the economic and political level, first in support of President Aristide's return, and now in support of the institution of democracy, have filled me with certain reservations concerning both the declared interests of democracy as such and the historic and geopolitical ends of such a movement within postcolonialism. This does not in any way mean that I take issue with the fact of democracy as such. For the time being—and, more than likely, for a long time to come—it is the best political regime that we have. Democracy is also unique in that its process contains the mechanisms for the very political changes it needs.

Jacques Lacan  

On the Movement of Truth in the Human Sciences

While theory in the physical sciences has never really escaped from the requirement of internal coherence at the very heart of knowledge (connaissance), the human sciences, because they form themselves through the very behaviors that constitute their object, cannot evade the question of their meaning or pretend that the answer doesn't impose itself in terms of truth.

That human reality implies this process of revelation is a fact that has enabled some people to think of history as a dialectic inscribed in matter; indeed, no “behaviorist” ritual of protection of the subject in relation to its object can castrate this truth of its creative and mortal point, and this fact makes scientists, who are dedicated to “pure” knowledge, responsible in the first instance. No one knows this better than psychoanalysts who, in the awareness of what their subjects confide to them as well as in the handling of behaviors conditioned by analytic technique, act through a revelation whose truth determines its efficacy.

Moreover, is not the search for truth what constitutes the object of criminology in the realm of judicial matters, and also what unifies its two aspects: the truth of the crime under its police aspect and the truth of the criminal under its anthropological aspect?

The problem my presentation will be concerned with today is: what can the technique that guides our dialogue with the subject and the notions that our experience has defined in psychology contribute to this research? My presentation is less concerned with stating the contribution of psychoanalysis to the study of delinquency—discussed in the other presentations—than with posing the legitimate limits of our contribution. My purpose is certainly not to propagate the letter of our doctrines without concern for method, but to rethink our doctrine, as we are advised to do constantly, in relation to a new object.

On the Sociological Reality of Crime and of the Law and on the Relation of Psychoanalysis to their Dialectical Foundation

Neither crime nor criminals are objects that can be conceived outside of their sociological reference. The saying, “It's the law that makes the sin,” remains true outside the eschatological perspective of Grace where Saint Paul formulated it. This saying is scientifically verified by the observation that there is no society that does not include a positive law, whether traditional or written, one of custom or of right. There is also no society in which every degree of transgression that defines crime does not appear in the group. The supposed “unconscious,” “forced,” “intuitive” obedience by the “primitive” to the rules of the group is an ethnological conception; it is the product of an imaginary insistence that has left its mark on many other conceptions of “origins,” and it is just as mythic as they are.

In the typical melodrama plot, the leading character is forced to make a choice and to experience a loss: he or she has to give up a person loved, choose between one person and another, betray the family, or even give up on love altogether. But a special kind of melodrama deals with the choice made between love and profession, especially the profession of music. This tension between sexual love and devotion to music is the theme of the film Rhapsody (Charles Vidor, 1954), which I will use as an example to clarify the connections among love, desire and drive in Lacanian psychoanalysis.

Rhapsody

The film starts with the young, rich Lulu (played by Elizabeth Taylor) accompanying her poor boyfriend Paul (Vittorio Gassman) to Zurich, where he has come to study the violin. Lulu quickly realizes that her lover is devoted first to music and that his love for her comes second. For this reason, they end their relationship after the big success of his first concert. Lulu then marries a pianist, James, who in his love for Lulu gives up on his career. However, as a result, he starts drinking, and Lulu comes to despise him. In Paris, Lulu once again meets Paul, whom she still loves, but he blames her for ruining James. To become worthy of Paul's love, Lulu decides to help James to continue with his study of music. She thus devotes herself to his career and forces him to practice. But before James's first concert, Lulu informs him that now that he has become a great pianist, she is going to abandon him for Paul. Heartbroken, James finishes the concert with great pain, but he does not give up—the concert is a great success. Lulu listens from the back row and is totally taken by James's performance. Paul waits for her, but she decides that she is not going with him, because she truly loves James.

The plot of this melodrama revolves around the problem that the subject is never loved in the way he or she would like to be. Both men, Paul and James, love Lulu in the way that she does not want to be loved. Thus, it first appears that Paul loves her too little and James too much. But Lulu also loves her men in the wrong way: in her love for Paul, she can allow no place for his devotion to music, and she initially does not love James at all but only wants his submissions in order to despise him for it. The paradox of the film is that Lulu starts loving James only at the moment when he is able to forget her and give himself to the music.

Throughout the 1980s a wave of books and anthologies appeared, written mainly by English professors, articulating psychoanalytic theory with other critical discourses and disciplines, such as feminism, literature, deconstruction, and film theory.1 So rapidly did these books become a recognizable and marketable genre that by 1990 an anthology could be titled simply Psychoanalysis and…. Even without a subtitle, Psychoanalysis and… presented no mystery—one had a fairly clear sense of what one was getting when one purchased it. A legacy of the theory wave in literary studies and part of the explosion of cultural studies in North America, these books elicited an oft-voiced concern that psychoanalysis, rather than encouraging authentic interdisciplinarity, might simply colonize other discourses, narcissistically finding its own reflection everywhere it turned.

One version of this concern—which Joan Copjec's new book answers—was expressed in the widespread objection that psychoanalytic theory tends toward ahistoricism, that by finding the same structures of desire in all cultures and periods psychoanalysis sloughs off historical specificity and overrides cultural differences. For this reason, critics often contend, psychoanalysis teaches us nothing about the historical period or culture under consideration, and everything about itself. In deference to this legitimate concern, anthologies and books articulating psychoanalysis with some other discourse became more or less adept at claiming that the other discourse—say, literature or feminism—was being used to interpret psychoanalysis as much as the reverse. For example, Shoshana Felman wrote in her introduction to an anthology titled Literature and Psychoanalysis, “In the same way that psychoanalysis points to the unconscious of literature, literature, in its turn, is the unconscious of psychoanalysis” (10). Psychoanalysis was warned to respect the “otherness”—the cultural difference or disciplinary specificity—of whatever it was interpreting. When this warning went unheeded, psychoanalytic methods were largely abandoned by self-respecting literary and cultural critics in favor of a stronger emphasis on archival research—an approach that promised to yield greater historical and cultural particularity. Thus the theory wave of the 1970s was followed by the new historicism of the 1980s, a partly reactive but highly productive phenomenon whose star is now waning—for reasons that Joan Copjec's Read My Desire enables us to understand.

The Lacanian Subject not only provides an excellent introduction into the fundamental coordinates of Jacques Lacan's conceptual network; it also proposes original solutions to (or at least clarifications of) some of the crucial dilemmas left open by Lacan's work. The principal two among them are the notion of “love beyond Law” mentioned by Lacan in the very last page of his Seminar XI,1 and the no less enigmatic thesis of the late Lacan according to which, at the end of psychoanalytic treatment, the subject becomes its own cause. Since these two points run against the predominant doxa on Lacan (love as a narcissistic misrecognition which obscures the truth of desire; the irreducibly decentered status of the subject), it is well worth the while to elaborate them.

“Love beyond Law” involves a “feminine” sublimation of drives into love. As Fink emphasizes again and again, love is here no longer merely a narcissistic (mis)recognition to be opposed to desire as the subject's “truth” but a unique case of direct asexual sublimation (integration into the order of the signifier) of drives, of their jouissance, in the guise of the asexual Thing (music, religion, etc.) experienced in the ecstatic surrender.2 What one should bear in mind apropos of this love beyond Law, this direct asexual sublimation of drive, is that it is inherently nonsensical, beyond meaning: meaning can only take place within the (symbolic) Law; the moment we tresspass the domain of Law, meaning changes into enjoymeant [jouis-sense].3

Insofar as, according to Lacan, at the conclusion of psychoanalytic treatment, the subject assumes the drive beyond fantasy and beyond (the Law of) desire, this problematic also compels us to confront the question of the conclusion of treatment in all its urgency. If we discard the discredited standard formulas (“reintegration into the symbolic space,” etc.), only two options remain open: desire or drive. That is to say, either we conceive the conclusion of treatment as the assertion of the subject's radical openness to the enigma of the Other's desire no longer veiled by fantasmatic formations, or we risk the step beyond desire itself and adopt the position of the saint who is no longer bothered by the Other's desire as its decentered cause. In the case of the saint, the subject, in an unheard-of way, “causes itself,” becomes its own cause. Its cause is no longer decentered—i.e., the enigma of the Other's desire no longer has any hold over it. How are we to understand this strange reversal on which Fink is quite justified to insist? In principle, things are clear enough: by way of positing itself as its own cause, the subject fully assumes the fact that the object-cause of its desire is not a cause that precedes its effects but is retroactively posited by the network of its effects: an event is never simply in itself traumatic, it only becomes a trauma retroactively, by being “secreted” from the subject's symbolic space as its inassimilable point of reference. In this precise sense, the subject “causes itself” by way of retroactively positing that X which acts as the object-cause of its desire. This loop is constitutive of the subject. That is, an entity that does not “cause itself” is precisely not a subject but an object.4 However, one should avoid conceiving this assumption as a kind of symbolic integration of the decentered Real, whereby the subject “symbolizes,” assumes as an act of its free choice, the imposed trauma of the contingent encounter with the Real. The Need for Enemies

How rapidly—and tragically—the celebration of freedom occasioned by throwing off the yoke of Communist rule in the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe was succeeded by a wave of ethnic/nationalist conflicts, expressed at its violent genocidal extreme in the identity war in Bosnia, in which ethnic cleansing became policy. Tragic, but predictable, for the loss of enemies is destabilizing, and the chaos left in the wake of the departing Communist enemy provided fertile soil for hate-mongering demagogues to exploit centuries-old hostilities.

The revival of hostility among existing groups with a history of conflict is not surprising. Nor, given the long-standing history of anti-Semitism in these nations, would it be surprising to see the revival of anti-Semitism in post-Communist eastern Europe, if there were Jews there. The fact that anti-Semitism has revived so powerfully in the absence of Jews demonstrates the power of the paranoid dynamic and the associated need for enemies. When the real enemy disappears, the need for enemies becomes intensified, and in the absence of real enemies they will be created.

There is a readiness in the human psyche to fear strangers and seek comfort with the familiar. Under duress, stranger anxiety and fear of the other mount, and the paranoid capacity to project hatred is mobilized. Such anxiety is produced not only by unknown persons, but also by unfamiliar places, foods, and sounds. Significant others—parents, teachers, peers—sponsor “suitable targets of externalization” for the developing child, and “group-specific externalizations” tie the children together (Volkan 32). The strangeness of some things (and the comforting familiarity of others) take on political significance as the child grows into adulthood.

This fear of the stranger and projection of hatred upon the other are the psychological foundation of the concept of the enemy.2 The crystallization of the shared comfort of the familiar is the psychological foundation of nationalism.

Introduction: Hybrid, Borderline Theories

The position of Latin America within today's geopolitical configuration is a highly ambiguous one.1 Unlike other regions commonly dubbed “postcolonial,” Latin America finds itself in the margins of not only the West but also of postcoloniality itself, or at least of postcolonial studies. The relatively few panels addressing Latin America at this conference,2 combined with the fact that, of the ten invited speakers, not one is a Latin Americanist—these rather banal facts attest to the odd relationship of Latin America and postcolonialism. In the following pages I will nonetheless resist the temptation of mapping Latin America onto the postcolonial expanse. Instead, I will evaluate certain aspects of postcoloniality via Latin America's peculiar position within the postcolonial scene.

Since much of my analysis will hinge on a notion of hybridity, it is necessary to define what I mean by this term. Hybridity, of course, has already established itself as a key notion within postcolonial studies, especially in the work of Homi Bhabha.3 My own ideas, in fact, will appear as quite similar to those of Bhabha; yet I will actually take my distance from Bhabha's work. For Bhabha, the oppression of colonized people and, by extension, the self-construction of the colonizer, are grounded on the West's aversion to its own fundamental multiplicity. Colonized peoples, dwelling both within and without the West, Western doubles but not quite Western, embody this hybridity. It is through the objectification or abjectification of the colonized Other (who by doubling the West, in fact splits it), then, that the West endlessly and violently attempts to forge a united origin and authenticity: a self uncontaminated and uncut (by outsiders, “foreigners,” Others).

Bhabha's theory of hybridity is also, therefore, a theory of displacement. For Bhabha, a voyage toward and through the land of another determines subjects from the start; a fusion with, and infusion of another's space—again, hybridity—and a movement away from the self belong to the structure of every subject. Violence against a scapegoated Other, who subversively stands for this general displacement process of which he/she is only an effect, is one way dominant peoples/cultures or oppressors viciously try to disavow these facts.
